speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On 13 March 2006, the media published my letter in which I said, "It would seem that there is much ambiguity in the Wild Animals and Birds Act and perhaps, it is time to improve and amend the law to make it a more effective tool in the protection of wild animals." In the past 14 years, we have focused on strengthening other animal-related legislation, including the Endangered Species (Import and Export) Act or ESA, the Animals and Birds Act or ABA, and the Parks and Trees Act or PTA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill drafted by people, and based on feedback and suggestions from the people.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This journey and this Bill has been made possible by the work of the Wild Animal Legislation Review Committee or WALRC.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the process of developing our recommendations, we recognised that different segments of society hold different views about wildlife protection and human-wildlife co-existence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Interest in animal welfare and nature conservation is growing and many regard the preservation of wildlife as a matter of critical importance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But there are others who are less comfortable with wildlife or who are primarily concerned about wildlife matters only as they relate to public health and safety.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We tried our best to capture as many of these views as possible.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We started with the composition of the committee itself, which comprises a wide cross-section of society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We not only have representatives from the nature and animal welfare community, but also from the Singapore Pest Management Association, the Pet Enterprise and Traders Association of Singapore, the Singapore Buddhist Federation, the academic and legal community, and the Nee Soon East Youth Network.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To supplement the committee's passion and expertise, we also conducted extensive public consultation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our goal was to hear from the people themselves and to gauge the level of support for our proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Perhaps, we should give some time for more Members to come in, because I do not believe we have a quorum.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I have sent a message out for them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The first public consultation was a face-to-face session in May 2018.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We took extra time to consult groups that had particular interests in some of the proposals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We held consultations with pest control companies in June 2018 and with religious organisations in June 2019.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Our final face-to-face public consultation was held in August 2019.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: There, we shared the proposed amendments and also explained why we did not proceed with some of the earlier proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In January 2020, we met with the MND Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) Members to obtain their feedback on the proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This two-year journey of public consultations has taught me and the other committee members a great deal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I think we now have a piece of law with the coolest name.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: With that, I will now outline the key features of WA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In the past 19 years, I have worked closely with NParks and previously, the AVA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We have worked hand-in-hand to protect animals in Singapore and safeguard their welfare and public safety.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I saw first-hand the gaps and how it was affecting our wildlife, public safety, the work of NParks and AVA officers, and NGOs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The feeding and release of wildlife is a good example.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Feeding wild animals in our parks is illegal and we advised her to stop, especially as the monkey had turned aggressive and started attacking other park users.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: However, instead of stopping, she started feeding the monkey at the apartments beside the park, where it was not illegal to feed wild animals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The Parks and Trees Act does not cover areas outside the parks and nature reserves.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: There was little NParks or ACRES could do to stop the feeding.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: She continued feeding the monkey and soon, residents started to complain, and eventually, we had to remove this wild monkey.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Unfortunately, this is not an isolated case and the feeding of wildlife happens regularly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It is also not just monkeys but a wide range of other animals, including wild boars and birds.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: First, it can alter wildlife behaviour, thus affecting public safety.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Again, for example, macaques who are used to being fed by humans can get aggressive if they think you are holding their next meal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Second, it can increase wildlife populations and cause disamenities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Anthropogenic food provisioning is a key driver of pigeon growth in urban areas.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Wild animals can get addicted to sugary human food.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This is not only bad for their health but also leads them to neglect vital ecological roles like seed dispersion.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: For birds in particular, outside of parks and nature reserves, our law prohibits only the feeding of pigeons, and not other birds.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This gap makes it harder for us to address the root of the problem when it comes to human-wildlife conflicts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We have rescued so many animals who had been released.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I cannot count the number of pig-nosed turtles that have turned up dead on our shores.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Many think they are marine turtles who live in the sea but they are actually freshwater turtles.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: They go through a very painful death when released into the sea.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: While we do our best to rescue these animals, many do not survive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In my speech on the Parks and Trees (Amendment) Bill, I shared my concerns about the current legislation and proposed to prohibit the release of animals anywhere, on land or in water, in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I proposed that we should not restrict these prohibitions to only certain areas.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Specifically, I said, "Animals are not stationary and have the freedom to travel from unrestricted areas to nature reserves.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Hence, I see little rationale in creating demarcations when prohibiting the release of animals." Sir, the release of animals poses many concerns as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: First, it is harmful to animal welfare as released animals who are not properly rehabilitated often do not survive in the wild.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Second, it can create health issues for both humans and the animals as released animals could introduce diseases into the environment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Third, it can pose a problem to public safety, in the case where dangerous animals like stingrays are released.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: And fourth, it can imbalance and threaten eco-systems as invasive species can harm our native populations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Today, there are existing controls in the PTA on the feeding and release of wildlife in our parks and nature reserves.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We acknowledge that the majority of people who feed or release animals do not do so for malicious reasons.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We consulted the relevant stakeholders, particularly religious groups, on how to achieve this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: For instance, we discussed alternatives to mercy release with local Buddhist organisations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We can build on and scale up what a Buddhist temple has practised by inviting pet owners to get their animals blessed and animal welfare charities to stage an adoption drive for strays.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The temple's spiritual director said, "Buying and releasing animals is actually not good for the environment, so it's much better if we can feed and re-home strays." Other ideas raised were volunteering at animal shelters or tree-planting.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The WALRC will continue to work with the community on education and outreach efforts surrounding feeding and release of wild animals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: One of the most common questions I have been asked over the past two decades is, "Singapore got wildlife meh".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Plenty of wildlife and our biodiversity in Singapore is amazing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Our wildlife lives in our parks and nature reserves where they receive protection under the PTA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But those who live outside parks and nature reserves also need similar protection as they can be targeted by poachers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The WALRC contemplated the need for stronger controls on nets and traps outside parks and nature reserves.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We were concerned about both the deliberate poaching of wildlife as well as incidental harm inflicted on wildlife caused by the inappropriate use of nets and traps.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In recent years, we have seen cases of our beloved otters being killed in traps near Changi Sailing Club and along Marina Promenade.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Currently, NParks can prosecute poachers for taking, or attempting to take, wildlife.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But it is still challenging for NParks to enforce against poachers as traps are often left unattended, or may simply be abandoned.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: So, instead of only focusing on how to catch and prosecute people, we asked ourselves: what more can we do to mitigate the harm to the public and wildlife caused by nets and traps?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We also wanted to more strongly deter the use of snare traps.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Snare traps use trigger-activated nooses to trap wildlife, often maiming or killing them in the process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: These are dangerous not only to wildlife but also to humans, especially young children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Another issue that the WALRC grappled with was whether all wildlife species should be equally protected under the Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: One day, I received a call informing me that the people keeping ants were very angry with me.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: To be honest, I never knew people kept ants as pets.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But actually and technically, I, too, keep ants as pets.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: My three little angels at home drop crumbs and food everywhere and we now have a fair number of ants living with us and lovingly fed by my daughters.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I do tell my daughters ants are our friends.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I was told the people were angry as I was proposing amendments to the law that will make the keeping of ants illegal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Ants are invertebrates and we had a huge discussion on how invertebrates should be treated under the Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: On one hand, there are threatened invertebrates like horseshoe crabs that should be protected.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But on the other hand, it seems excessive to disallow people from killing animals like cockroaches, or trapping and keeping insects for leisure or educational purposes, such as ant-keeping or teaching kids about animal life cycles.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The Bill provides for a calibrated approach to be taken in cases like this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This means that some activities that do not undermine the overall aim of wildlife protection could be carved out.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Using section 20, I understand that MND will exempt pests and non-threatened invertebrates from protection against killing and trapping.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: However, we should not exclude invertebrates from the Act altogether.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: For example, we should not allow the unregulated import or release of dangerous or invasive invertebrates, such as the venomous bulldog ant or invasive fire ants, which could wreak havoc on our eco-system and cause harm to the public.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: There will be additional safeguards to ensure that threatened invertebrates are adequately protected.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Most of these threatened invertebrates are already living in our parks and nature reserves, and today, it is already an offence to kill or trap them under the current PTA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The Bill additionally empowers the Minister to prescribe a new list of "protected wildlife species".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In summary, you can keep ants as pets and you can trap them outside of parks and nature reserves.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But if you plan to import, trap them within nature reserves or trap selected threatened invertebrates, you will need NParks' approval.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Ninety percent of respondents on the REACH consultation agreed with this broad approach and felt that at least threatened invertebrates should be protected from killing, keeping or capturing without a permit throughout Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: That said, we are aware that some may accidentally or unknowingly violate the rules, especially if they are less familiar with wildlife.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The WALRC and NParks will work with stakeholders on public awareness campaigns, and I trust that NParks will enforce the law fairly and reasonably.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We move on now to the question of penalties.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The penalties under the current Act are far too low to deter would-be poachers and traffickers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Some of these animals fetch much more on the black market.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Clause 7 also introduces heavier penalties for animal-related businesses that kill, trap, take or keep wildlife.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This is necessary because first, these businesses are capable of causing much more harm than individual offenders, as in the case of a wildlife management company illegally killing or trapping wildlife.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Second, these businesses have a stronger duty of care towards animals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Third, businesses are generally more financially capable of paying fines, so a higher fine quantum is needed as a stronger deterrent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The definition of "animal-related business" is the same as the one in ABA, which also includes animal welfare groups like ACRES.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: There will also be higher penalties for repeat and recalcitrant offenders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The proposed penalty structure has two tiers, with one tier for first convictions, and another tier for second and subsequent convictions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We saw a further need to more strongly protect certain native threatened wildlife species, similar to how the ESA more strongly protects globally threatened species listed under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Take the Sunda pangolin, for example, which is both CITES-listed and native to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Clause 2 thus introduces "protected wildlife species" to be prescribed by the Minister.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I understand that MND intends to take reference from the CITES Appendices and the Singapore Red Data Book in putting together this list of protected species.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But this is not to say that every species found in those lists will automatically be prescribed on the protected wildlife species list.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I understand that MND and NParks will develop a robust selection criteria.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The general principle will be that the protected wildlife species list will contain native species that are domestically threatened.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I hope that the list will be progressively refined and amended in consultation with experts and the nature community.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Take, for example, a development project that is near a known wildlife habitat.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: If the developer had deliberately killed a wild animal to make way for works, it would be an offence under the existing WABA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: If the animal was killed in a nature reserve, it would be an offence also under the PTA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In addition, as part of the EIA requirements, NParks might have required the developer to install hoardings to prevent wildlife from venturing out onto the roads.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: However, if the developer failed to do so and the wild animal walked onto a road straight into the path of an unwitting motorist, there is currently limited recourse under the law.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I am glad to share that after discussions with MND and NParks, we will have a new section 10 that will empower the Director-General, Wildlife Management to issue directions to developers to carry out wildlife-related measures to safeguard wildlife, public health or safety, or the health of the eco-system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This would give the EIA process additional "teeth" and serve as a stronger incentive for developers to comply with EIA conditions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Clauses 10 to 15 would largely align NParks' powers under the Wildlife Act with those under the ABA and ESA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This includes allowing NParks to direct people to pay the costs of repatriating smuggled wildlife in a way that ensures that the wildlife is properly cared for.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This is so the Government does not have to bear the costs of repairing the damage caused by smugglers, and is similar to the existing powers in the ESA, for dealing with smuggled wildlife species.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We also propose a new power for the Court to be able to forfeit conveyances used in the commission of a convicted offence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The risk of losing their vehicles would serve as a stronger deterrent to would-be smugglers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Nonetheless, we recognise that there must be safeguards to expanded powers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: My heartfelt thanks to: Karen Sim, the Secretary of the committee; Kalai Vanan from ACRES; Daryl Yeo from the Nature Photographic Society; Kerry Pereira from the Nature Society Singapore; Wong Jin Feng from the Nee Soon East Youth Network; Joseph Chun from the Faculty of Law at NUS; N Sivasothi from the Department of Biological Sciences at NUS; Matthew Lim from the Pet Enterprise Traders Association of Singapore; Venerable Shi You Guang from the Singapore Buddhist Federation; Ng Say Kiat from the Singapore Pest Management Association; Jaipal Singh from the SPCA; the late Subaraj Rajathurai from Strix Wildlife Consultancy; Jessica Lee from the Wildlife Reserves Singapore; Ria Tan from WildSingapore and my team of Legislative Assistants.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I would also like to thank NParks and MND for their views and suggestions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: NParks served as a resource panel to the WALRC.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This helped us better plan out which wildlife protection outcomes would be better achieved via legislation and which should be done via other means.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We worked to ensure that the proposals were practical and could be implemented on the ground by NParks later on.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: MND and NParks also made some suggestions for additional amendments, some of which are contained in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I also want to specially thank Minister Desmond, Minister Lawrence and Senior Parliamentary Secretary Xueling for all their guidance and support for this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Last but certainly not least, a big thank you to members of the public for speaking up, for your thoughtful suggestions and constructive criticisms.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In the recent Netflix documentary series "Night on Earth", actress Samira Wiley narrates the episode on the impact of urban development on wildlife.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In episode 5, she describes Singapore as "one of the most wildlife-friendly cities on Earth".

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Wildlife is the beloved otter families in Bishan and the Marina Bay It is the long-tailed macaque that call our nature reserves home, and even the hornbills that have recently be seen perched on balconies in our homes.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Some have great affection for these wildlife creatures.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Others find them to be a nuisance or have a sense of suspicion and fear.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This can lead to great conflict as we have seen in the cases of bird feeders against their neighbours.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Other times, our affection for wildlife may lead to greater harm and nuisance to both animals and humans when our affection is expressed in uninformed ways.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This happens, for instance, when individuals feed wildlife inappropriately or capture animals for amusement and enjoyment without concern for what is natural for the animal.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Sugar gliders, pangolins and hedgehogs come to mind.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Wildlife should be integrated into our society and be part of what makes us uniquely Singapore, and not create conflict.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The new Wildlife Act is not just about telling us what to do or not to do in relation to wildlife.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: More than that, it is about learning how to interact with and enjoy our natural environment in a respectful and humane way.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I support the Bill and I have just a few comments.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I could imagine people using excuses of feeding "domestic" animals as a means to excuse themselves from this ruling.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It might be a small loophole, but a loophole nonetheless.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Currently, section 5(1) of WABA makes it an offence for any person to kill, take or keep wildlife without a permit.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The new offence requires the additional element of intention which, as before, the state has to prove.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is a high bar, as one could be trying to trap a pesky rat but, inadvertently, catch a Southeast Asian Shrew, a rare forest native.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The intent of the matter is hard to prove and we should consider removing that requirement.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Instead, we should educate our people to not trap, hunt or kill wildlife, and instead call upon professionals to get it done.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As we inevitably encroach into the spaces of wildlife, they, too, will move into ours.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: How we structure our laws will help to protect one from the other.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The intent of the two points above is not to nitpick at language but, rather, to find a specific set of actions we want to discourage, as we learn to share our common spaces with wildlife and put clear boundaries on what should and should not be done.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Currently, section 10(1) provides that " o person shall import into Singapore any wild animal or bird whether alive or dead, or any part thereof" except with written authorisation.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In the past, illegal wildlife parts like bearclaws, pangolins and other wildlife were part of folk remedies and traditional supplements and cures.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is vital that we continue to find new ways to interact with our environment.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As we build up new housing estates, new places of leisure, we need to learn to share these spaces with wildlife that was indigenous to that space.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: A strong set of laws and regulations will help to clarify the boundaries in which we can interact and share experiences with our rich and diverse wildlife.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: These clarifications notwithstanding, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is also a popular transit point for migratory birds.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even to this day, scientists and naturalists are finding out more and more about the treasure we have living among nature in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I wish to commend Mr Louis Ng for tabling this Bill in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the Southern Islands, there are sandy white beaches; there is an eco-system of coral reefs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are fascinating sea creatures, such as sea sponges and sea horses.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On land, rare birds and animals have been spotted in places like the Bukit Timah Nature Reserve.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some examples are the great slaty woodpecker and the mousedeer.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This piece of legislation shines a spotlight on the importance of wildlife to humanity, here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But there is a risk that the law becomes over-inclusive.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, would it hamper or prevent the extermination of pests, such as termites, cockroaches and silver fish?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I certainly hope Singaporeans will not be prevented from exterminating pests and rodents.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Having said this, this change has also provided for the important inclusion of invertebrates, such as star fish, sea cucumbers, horseshoe crabs and sea sponges – all creatures that inhabit Chek Jawa on Pulau Ubin.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I understand from news reports that the Singapore Pest Association has been consulted in the process of drafting this Bill.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My question to Mr Louis Ng is, has the Director-General also been consulted?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I hope that in and amongst these changes, Singaporeans will still, indeed, be permitted to exterminate pests, such as termites.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another way in which the Bill makes the Wild Animals and Birds Act more comprehensive is by including trapping under the law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is good that this gap is being plugged.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Additionally, this Bill makes the enforcement of the Act more robust.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are also enhanced penalties for animal-related business owners if they were to kill, trap, take or keep wildlife without written approval.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is good that, along with the increase in potential punishments under the offences of the Act that directly impact wildlife, the Bill also increases the punishment for certain offences that hinder certain investigations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Under the current section 12(3), failing to comply with a request for a name and address or for giving a false name or incomplete address to the officer could lead to a fine of up to $1,000 upon conviction.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The reason why I am asking this is because there is an argument to be made that enforcement officers interacting with and arresting the accused and investigating the crime should not be the same ones with the power to compound.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In	conclusion, Sir, I	thank	my	colleague	Mr	Louis	Ng	for tabling this Private Member's Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I join the hon Member Mr Christopher de Souza in congratulating the hon Member for Nee Soon, Mr Louis Ng, for leading the efforts to review the Wild Animals and Birds Act and moving this amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Louis Ng highlighted a 14-year journey in his speech delivered in his characteristic passionate style.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I applaud the fact that he and his members of the Wild Animals Legislation Review Committee had conducted extensive consultation over two years before tabling this Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I support the Bill in principle and would like to raise three points for clarification.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The first point is on a possible overlap between the Animals and Birds Act and the amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If my understanding is correct, may I please ask: what are the circumstances in which the different provisions would be invoked?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I can see the attraction of using the powers under this amendment Bill because there would be no need to distinguish between the birds which will satisfy the definition of "wildlife" and there will be less enforcement issues on the ground as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note from the amendment Bill, as currently worded, that the feeding and releasing of wildlife is punishable by sentences or fine.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do appreciate, as Mr Louis Ng mentioned, that the proposed fine quantums are higher.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is a carve-out for Community Work Orders (CWOs) though.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This may be a good sentencing option in some cases, particularly for those who caused disamenities, such as making public places dirty.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Unfortunately, it does not appear that they can be imposed with MTOs such that the underlying causes of the offending behaviour may be treated so as to reduce the risk of them re-offending.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I will be grateful for clarification on the sentencing policies for such offenders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I support the criminalisation of feeding and releasing of wildlife.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Louis Ng again eloquently explained the raison d'etre for this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There are occasions, however, where a person's feeding or releasing of wildlife is an act of kindness.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Take the case of a person who comes across a wounded eagle which crashed into a glass door.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The person, out of concern for the eagle, may feed it and then release it thereafter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Such acts would not change wildlife behaviour, nor would it cause disamenities or ecological degradation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That is the mischief that Mr Louis Ng highlighted in relation to criminalising acts of feeding and releasing wildlife.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But, technically, these persons may have committed such offences, granted the prosecution may exercise discretion not to prosecute.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But such people may eventually not take a risk of offending.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, this may not be consonant with the aims of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note that under the proposed section 5(1) of the amendment Bill, the Director-General will have powers to give written approval generally to a class of persons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And, if so, what would be the conditions?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: He spent the last two years working with the Wild Animal Legislation Review Committee on the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We know there are real risks of disease transmission between wildlife and humans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, maintaining the right balance between wildlife and human activity is not only good for the environment, it is also good for ourselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I have two broad concerns about the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The first concerns the practices that harm wildlife or the eco-system, such as the feeding and release of wildlife and trafficking.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For this, my questions are on whether the penalties proposed in the Bill are appropriate and how will enforcement be carried out.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The second concerns the Bill's granting of powers to the Director-General to direct development or works to implement measures to safeguard wildlife.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: My questions are on how we can achieve the right balance between the protection of wildlife and eco-systems and the need to develop land and natural resources for the benefit of society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I will direct questions on the principles behind the Bill to Mr Louis Ng, and questions on policy implementation to the Ministry.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I will start with the feeding and release of wildlife.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Today, I think the public is generally aware that feeding wildlife threatens the eco-system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It also poses a risk to public health and safety if wildlife is encouraged to interact with humans through feeding.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The question is whether the penalties in the Bill and the enforcement framework are proportionate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Could Mr Louis Ng explain his thinking about whether the offence should be compoundable and what he thinks should guide sentencing if a case happens to be prosecuted in Court?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In what circumstances does Mr Louis Ng think the Director-General should grant written approval for feeding wildlife?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For the Ministry, I wish to ask to what extent feeding wildlife will be regulated in practice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Will issuing summons for feeding wildlife be part of regular enforcement activity, or is it more a measure of last resort against people who cannot be convinced to stop feeding wildlife?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Next, the proposed section 5B governs the release of wildlife.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is a sensitive issue because some people release wildlife as part of celebrations or religious practices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Ng has shared his many discussions with religious groups on this matter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The potential harm that such releases cause also depends on what wildlife people are releasing and where they do it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Could Mr Ng share his thinking on how we can use this Bill to sensitively address this issue of wildlife release in religious practices?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There may yet be other groups out there whom he has not been able to reach out to yet.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For the Ministry, I wish to ask what we have learnt from existing enforcement efforts on wildlife released in nature reserves and how this will be extended to wildlife released in other areas after this Bill is passed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Next, the proposed sections 11B and 12C grant powers of seizure and forfeiture over articles and conveyances connected to offences under the Act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Only very large vehicles are exempt from forfeiture, as Mr Ng pointed out.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For example, a private boat operator who transports wildlife for unauthorised release in the sea could face a risk of having his boat seized and forfeited.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I wish to ask Mr Ng how he thinks these powers should be limited for the seizure of conveyances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The seizure of vehicles involved in smuggling – I think that is a widely accepted principle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But does Mr Ng intend that if someone were to drive their car to feed or release wildlife, should their car be seizeable under the Act?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, how should vehicles hired out for passengers or cargo be treated?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, would Mr Ng agree that passenger or cargo hire vehicles should not be seizeable or forfeitable unless the owner or operator was reckless or abetted offences under the Act?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If he agrees on this, then does he think that the Bill, as currently written, really limits the powers of seizure and forfeiture sufficiently?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I know Mr Ng has noted that owners of vehicles are not at risk if the offences were committed without their consent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But the question is: what is the burden of proof here?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It may be impractical for many vehicle owners to thoroughly investigate the intention of their hirers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, I believe that providers of small-scale passenger or cargo services are actually in need of statutory protection from seizure or forfeiture under this Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: To me, it is actually somewhat odd that protection is to be given to the large vehicles, which I do not think would be in our public interest to seize, but not to the smaller vehicles at all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Next, the proposed section 10 of the Act will grant the Director-General power to issue directions to require development works to implement measures to safeguard wildlife, public safety or the eco-system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Section 10(4) does allow a person to refuse to comply with a Direction if they have a reasonable excuse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Does Mr Ng think that this is sufficient protection against an unreasonable direction and what principles determine whether an excuse is or is not reasonable?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I do not know if the amended Act is capable of being used as such.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But, to me, this seems a bit too important to leave to judicial interpretation alone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Does the Director-General have a staff that is capable of conducting environmental cost-benefit analysis?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If not, will that staff be created and trained to exercise these powers?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: How will the Director-General engage stakeholders, such as environmental interest groups as well as developers, to ensure that any directions issued respect both environmental concerns and development matters?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: However, we must ensure that the public agrees this Bill's measures, when enforced, are fair, reasonable and proportionate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We must also acknowledge that with limited resources, we have to balance protecting wildlife and the eco-system with human development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is very fashionable to say that we can have both, but that is actually a fantasy unless we can change how we define human development to mean that we should reduce our footprint and our impact on the natural world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: That could mean halting or reversing our population and consumption growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I do not think we have a consensus on that yet as a society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But, with respect, I am not sure they can all be addressed without altering the legislation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: However, I remain open to hearing Mr Ng and the Ministry's replies to my concerns.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have previously filed a Parliamentary Question about the illegal smuggling of pet birds and also spoke at length about the caged birds trade during MND's Committee of Supply last month.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, cats and dogs are domesticated species and are perfectly happy living alongside humans.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On the other hand, most birds are caught from the wild by poachers deploying very inhumane methods.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As Uncle Ben said to Spiderman, "With great power, comes great responsibility." What we allow our consumers to buy affects the wildlife in our region.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I go to the wet market regularly and am shocked to see baby pomfrets, which are smaller than the size of my palm, being sold – and I do not have big palms.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Without giving the chance for juvenile fish to grow, it can only result in the eventual depletion and extinction of many fish species.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A longer term solution will require us to engage our regional neighbours and they would need to get the necessary buy-in from fishermen who depend on fishing for their livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But, Sir, we can harness our relatively higher purchasing power and turn it into a force for good.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: By disallowing the sale of juvenile fish, we are sending a strong signal and reducing the incentive for the catching of such juvenile fish.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a nation, we can set an example of how we can make the world a better place for all species.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We can certainly do more to protect wildlife here, preserve our natural heritage and ensure their survival.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is necessary for a healthy, flourishing eco-system.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have been most assured by the involvement of the public and various stakeholders, including concerned nature- and pet-lovers and even pest control companies, who provided their valuable feedback and suggestions for this Bill.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   I welcome the amendments to the Wild Animals and Birds Act, particularly the new section 5A.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This part stipulates that unless permission was given by the authorities, no person will be permitted to intentionally feed any wildlife in any place.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Otherwise, he will be deemed guilty of an offence.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In our garden city, it is natural to have birdsong and the fragrance of flowers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But there are many wild birds in my constituency.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have received complaints from many residents that they are faced with the problems of noise and bird droppings caused by large flocks of wild birds.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Stopping the feeding of wild birds should reduce the food supply for them and hence, reduce their numbers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But how effective this provision will be is still unknown.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition to punishing those who deliberately feed birds, serious penalties should also be given to residents and businesses who litter and treat food waste carelessly, as these foods are an important source of survival for wild birds and pests.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I call on the Minister to curb the over-feeding of wild birds in residential areas, to address their pollution problems and to reduce the risk of possible transmission of diseases.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The amendments to the Wild Animals and Birds Act have been a long time coming for more stringent measures needed to give more protection to wildlife beyond nature parks and reserves, and for more severe enforcement to deter offenders of abuse, exploitation and killing of wildlife.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Urban wildlife continues to face challenges with unabated development in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: But I am heartened that we have become more considered in promoting nature-based solutions and increasing ecological connectivity within urban spaces in recent years.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill is, therefore, timely and welcomed in back-boning this City in Nature vision with appropriate legislative interventions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The first relates to the definition of "wildlife" in relation to marine species.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I note clause 4 of the Bill amends the definition of "wildlife" in section 2 of the principal Act which also "includes any mammal, bird, reptile, amphibian, fish or invertebrate, whether of wild nature or otherwise".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that wild marine animals are traded and exchanged freely by SEA Aquarium Singapore.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The re-enacted sections 8 and 9 of the Bill prohibits the sale, including offer for sale, or export of any living or dead wildlife or import of any living wildlife respectively without the Director-General's written approval.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Under what circumstances will the Director-General give the approval for importation and trade, and will this approval come only after a board is consulted or will it come about through absolute veto power?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Whilst we are on the prohibition on trading of marine wildlife, dead or alive, Mr Speaker, I would like to also take this opportunity to raise the issue of importation of shark species.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Our existing Harmonised System (HS) classification of goods does not include enough differentiation on shark species being imported.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: A 2017 report on sharks and ray trade in Singapore by Traffic, a leading NGO working globally on trade in wild animals and plants in the context of both biodiversity conservation and sustainable development, found that the shark commodity categories that are reported to the Food & Agriculture Organisation of the United Nations (FAO) do not completely match with the Singapore Trade Classification, Customs and Excise Duties (STCCED) codes for shark products.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For avoidance of doubt, can the Member confirm that the "authorised officer" referred to in section 10A could also include any ordinary citizen so authorised and given power to remove and dismantle traps that they find in keeping with the spirit of citizen empowerment?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, it is not clear if offenders will be subsequently prosecuted if they are confronted at the scene by the authorised officer.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Last but not least, Mr Speaker, my third point relates to the alignment of this Bill with the Parks and Trees Act.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Section 10(1) of the Bill states that the Director-General may direct a person to take wildlife-related measures to safeguard the health and safety of any wildlife, public health or safety in relation to wildlife or the health of the eco-system.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Given the proposed provisions, in the event that a nature reserve is de-gazetted in order for the land to be used for development, can the Minister clarify if section 10(1) will come into effect to halt the development?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In a 2019 study on the protection of nature reserves under the Parks and Trees Act, the question on the depth to which nature reserves are protected was raised.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The report said, I quote, "Humans are transforming Earth's natural landscapes so dramatically that as many as one million plant and animal species are now at risk of extinction." This Bill is a great green leap forward in the right direction for wildlife protection and legislation in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Wildlife belongs to no one; any exploitation and abuse by anyone should not be tolerated.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For the last few weeks, a mummy yellow vented bulbul built her nest on my tall cordy plant in the little garden outside my HDB flat and laid two eggs which I hope have birthed into two healthy little hatchlings.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I have left them alone and have, in fact, tiptoed around them so they feel safe!

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This might be a glimpse of living in our City in Nature that Minister Desmond Lee envisioned.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Because the wildlife and its habitat cannot speak, so we must.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I look forward to the clarifications from the Member and the Minister.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: NParks served as a resource panel to the WALRC, and we are glad for the opportunity to also engage with the community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Despite our small size, Singapore is home to a wide range of flora and fauna.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Our efforts to nurture a City in a Garden have allowed biodiversity to thrive.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Many Singaporeans delight in seeing once-rare wildlife, such as otters, in Singapore's rivers and canals.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Besides intensifying nature and greenery in our parks and gardens, this will also include efforts to conserve important plant and wildlife species in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will implement these plans together with Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I am heartened to see that Singaporeans of all ages and walks of life are becoming more passionate about nature conservation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Many have stepped forward to volunteer with NParks.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I hope that those who responded to the WALRC's public consultation exercise will also similarly lend their support to our City in Nature initiatives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: MND notes that many members of the public expressed broad support for the WALRC's proposals, but there were also differing views.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For example, how best to rationalise the need for strong legislation, while avoiding being excessively harsh to people who may be unaware or well-meaning?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This means that we must take a balanced approach and build awareness among Singaporeans on how to co-exist harmoniously with animals, including wildlife.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked how NParks will enforce the prohibition against intentional feeding of wildlife and curb the over-breeding of wild birds in residential areas.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I believe this also addresses Assoc Prof Walter Theseira's question on the enforcement of section 5A of the Wildlife Act.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To further clarify, NParks can already enforce against the feeding of wildlife in parks and nature reserves under the Parks and Trees Act.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Wildlife Act extends these powers beyond these areas.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This allows NParks to address the disamenities and ecological impact brought about from wildlife feeding in a more comprehensive manner across Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As for wild birds that cause disamenities, we agree with Mr Gan's observation that reducing anthropogenic food supply, whether from intentional feeding, littering or food waste, will help prevent these birds from being attracted to residential areas and moderate their population.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In this regard, NParks has already been working closely with other Government agencies and Town Councils on measures to reduce feeding of birds.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will continue to take a balanced approach, involving a range of measures spanning from education and outreach to enforcement action, to address these issues comprehensively.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: NParks conducts public outreach events and puts up advisories and notices, in order to raise public awareness of the issue.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: NEA works with food centres and coffee shops in HDB estates to enforce against littering and to ensure proper management of food waste.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: On a related note, Mr Murali Pillai asked about the possible overlap between the Animals and Birds (Pigeons) Rules and the Wildlife Act.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In addition, Mr Murali asked about the sentencing options for feeding and releasing wildlife.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As he noted, this comes under the Criminal Procedure Code, and we will need to study this together with MinLaw.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Nonetheless, NParks is already aware that some feeders may have underlying conditions or face certain circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This is done in collaboration with partners, such as Town Councils, grassroots leaders and social service organisations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We agree that beyond the legislative lever, there are various solutions to managing disamenities due to feeding, such as identifying and addressing underlying conditions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will continue to take a reasonable, multi-pronged approach to manage such issues.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Mr Murali also asked whether the Director-General (Wildlife Management) could issue a general written approval to people who feed and release wildlife as an act of kindness.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Instead of issuing a blanket approval, let me again assure the Member that NParks will take a reasonable approach to assess each situation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I will also encourage members of the public to call NParks' wildlife hotline when they come across wildlife in distress.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: While we appreciate the kindness behind trying to help wildlife, sometimes, feeding or releasing them may cause even more harm to the animal.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: From NParks' experience, strong engagement of stakeholders is an important means of effecting behavioural change.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For instance, it has been working with PUB on the annual Operation No Release to discourage people from releasing animals into ecologically sensitive areas like nature parks, nature reserves and reservoirs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Moving forward, NParks also plans to work with religious communities to explore alternatives to mercy release, such as tree planting and volunteering at animal shelters.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: So, NParks intends to continue with this approach of engagement and education as a key complement to legislation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Assoc Prof Theseira also asked when the Director-General may grant written approval to feed wildlife.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As mentioned, each situation will be assessed on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Mr Yee Chia Hsing spoke about the pet bird trade and how NParks ensures traceability of these birds.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I agree with Mr Yee that stopping the illegal import and smuggling of pet birds is important.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: That is why NParks has a suite of measures to detect and enforce against the illegal import and smuggling of birds today.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For example, NParks works closely with Singapore Customs, ICA and international partners to prevent instances of illegal bird imports at our borders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: And NParks’ measures do not stop at ensuring that pet birds are not smuggled into Singapore illegally.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Pet bird shops are licensed by NParks, and are required to comply with licensing requirements.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The source, date of arrival and date of purchase of each bird must be available.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Furthermore, the pet shop must also have CITES permits for any CITES-listed species which is regulated by the Endangered Species (Import and Export) Act.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Mr Yee also spoke about curbing the import and sale of juvenile fish.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As Mr Yee has noted, this is not something that Singapore can address on our own.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: While Singaporeans can be persuaded not to buy juvenile fish through public education, it is really up to individual countries to manage their own fish stocks sustainably.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In addition, we should also be conscious about the trade-offs in imposing additional regulations on our food supply.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This is something that MEWR and the Singapore Food Agency would be better placed to address.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Ms Anthea Ong asked about how the Wildlife Act relates to the trade of wild marine animals.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To clarify, commercial aquariums, including the SEA Aquarium, are currently regulated under the Animals and Birds Act and Endangered Species (Import and Export) Act.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: NParks will continue to use these Acts to regulate trade in a manner that ensures animal health and as required by the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, CITES for short.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Wildlife Act will complement the existing regime, especially with regard to non-CITES wildlife.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Director-General will consider factors like public safety and potential impact to our domestic eco-systems when making decisions on restricted activities pertaining to trade.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Ms Ong asked for a review of shark and ray trade information that is collected by agencies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As mentioned, our approach is to regulate wildlife trade in line with CITES requirements.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Singapore is a signatory to CITES, which is the main international agreement that aims to ensure that trade in wildlife does not threaten their survival.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Thus, when species are listed for protection under CITES, we create product codes accordingly.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Species-specific product codes are used for tracking the import and export of those species to ensure that there is sustainable trade.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As for the FAO’s shark commodity reporting categories, we understand that CITES already takes them into account and into consideration in formulating its lists.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As such, we will continue to review the collection and reporting of wildlife trade information in line with CITES requirements.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To Miss Cheng Li Hui’s query, I hope that this also clarifies that we are already abiding by CITES requirements in the regulation of wildlife trade – both imports and exports, and not just of live animals but also of parts and derivatives of animals.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Assoc Prof Theseira and Ms Ong asked a number of questions about the proposal to empower NParks’ Director-General (Wildlife Management) to issue wildlife-related directions to developers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: MND and NParks were involved extensively in the development of this proposal.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Assoc Prof Theseira asked if the amended Act grants private parties the right to sue the Director-General to issue directions on development works, perhaps with the aim of derailing large-scale Government development works.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The amendments introduced by the Bill do not change this existing position under the Act.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Second, the Director-General may issue directions to both private entities and public agencies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Wildlife Act does not mandate that the Director-General must take action under section 10(1).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To address Assoc Prof Theseira’s concerns, allow me to further put this provision in context.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Today, we already have a robust planning evaluation process in place for new developments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Regulatory agencies assess issues, such as public needs, economic and social considerations, and the impact on the environment, traffic, maritime navigation and so on.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We consider a wide range of factors, including the impact on the environment, in weighing the costs and benefits of any development project.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Development projects near sensitive nature areas are subject to additional scrutiny through an in-depth consultation process with relevant technical agencies, including NParks.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Through this, we may require developers to undertake thorough environmental studies and implement monitoring and mitigation plans.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: All environmental impact assessments include an Environmental Management and Monitoring Plan (EMMP), which comprises recommendations for specific measures that developers should undertake to manage potential impacts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Assoc Prof Theseira asked about the element of proportionality.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will take a sensible approach to imposing conditions under the EIA process.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Director-General will not unilaterally jeopardise development projects by imposing costly pigeon protection measures, for instance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Some more realistic examples of common wildlife-related conditions include requiring developers to install hoarding or limit works to daytime hours in certain areas to minimise impact to nocturnal wildlife.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We recognise that developers may have reasonable excuses to not comply with the Director-General’s directions, and have provided for this in the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For example, certain measures may turn out to not be technically feasible due to unforeseen changes in the ground situation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: NParks will work with developers to ensure that the wildlife-related measures under the EMMPs remain relevant and implementable.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Assoc Prof Theseira asked how the Director-General will exercise this power and if the relevant stakeholders will be engaged to ensure that the directions balance environmental concerns and developmental measures.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: NParks has staff that are trained to assess developers' EMMPs and advise developers further on how to implement them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This will ensure that the measures implemented on the ground are sensible and effective for the particular site context.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In the process, relevant stakeholders, such as nature groups, are consulted.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Ms Ong also asked whether section 10(1) of the Wildlife Act could halt a development.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Bill does not deal with the stopping of developments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Instead, it allows the Director-General to direct a developer to implement wildlife-related measures that the Director-General considers to be necessary to protect wildlife, public safety and so on.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The proposed penalties serve as a strong deterrent against non-compliance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Furthermore, this new power under the Wildlife Act does not stand alone; it is part of a broader framework that ensures that the environmental impact of developmental works is minimised.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As to Ms Ong’s question on the Central Catchment Nature Reserve, it is protected under the Parks and Trees Act (PTA) and its accompanying regulations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The PTA applies to underground activities, regardless of depth, which adversely affect the biodiversity and enjoyment of the Nature Reserve.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: However, if the underground activities are carried out at a depth that does not affect the biodiversity and enjoyment of the Nature Reserve, the PTA does not prevent such activities from being carried out.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As the administrator of both the PTA and the Wildlife Act, NParks will take a holistic approach in applying the Acts to developments that may impact wildlife, both within and outside the nature reserves.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Members asked about how NParks would operationalise the enforcement of the Wildlife Act’s provisions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Ms Ong asked whether offenders under the Wildlife Act would be prosecuted if they are confronted at the scene of the offence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As with all cases of suspected offences, NParks will first carry out investigations to ascertain the facts of the case.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Based on these facts, the appropriate enforcement actions, which could include prosecution, will be considered.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Assoc Prof Theseira asked about the composition of offences.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked for clarification on the term "authorised officers".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This term has the same meaning throughout the Act, whether referring to officers authorised to compound offences, or to those who interact with, investigate and arrest accused persons.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: That said, operationally, the Director-General will authorise different groups of officers for different functions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This Act is an important step towards improving wildlife protection, in partnership with key stakeholders and the community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Legislation is but one lever to do so.
