speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We should continue to ramp up public education and outreach efforts so that there is a sustained change in mindset which will allow us to live harmoniously with wildlife in our City in Nature.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for National Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I look forward to Mr Ng and the WALRC’s continued commitment to work with the wider nature community to spearhead such efforts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I will then address the points made by Members in this House and members of the public.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I will also share the concerns raised by people who do not support this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This is an outdated piece of legislation that permitted individuals to keep certain wildlife as pets, so long as they obtained a licence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But these animals clearly should not be privately owned.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Commercial animal establishments, such as zoos, will continue to be regulated under the Animals and Birds Act (ABA).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Second, the WALRC proposed ensuring that only trained and qualified individuals can kill and trap wildlife.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: There was strong public support for this in our consultations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Wildlife management can be risky, such as when workers need to handle snakes in a crowded area.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We felt that these workers should be trained to protect wildlife, the public and themselves.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Specifically, section 43 of the ABA already empowers the Director-General, Animal Health and Welfare, to specify training and qualification requirements for those engaging in prescribed animal-related businesses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I understand that NParks intends to implement this proposal in time and that it will take a phased approach to ensure that the industry has time to adjust, by first focusing on training and capacity building before imposing any formal regulatory requirements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Third, the WALRC proposed having codes of conduct for general activities in nature areas, such as wildlife photography, hiking and camping.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: There was also strong public support for this but many felt that, for now, these need not be made into laws to be enforced by the authorities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In this regard, the WALRC will work with the community to improve public education on wildlife-related measures.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Fourth, the WALRC had initially proposed to remove the Schedule of Specified Wild Animals and Birds, which currently exempts six bird species from protection against killing, trapping and keeping.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: These are the house crow, feral pigeon, common myna, white-vented myna, purple-backed starling and the Philippine glossy starling.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: There were public concerns about this and we decided that we will review this again at a later stage.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: For now, the Schedule will be moved into subsidiary legislation and MND will review the list of birds within it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: However, this was the least supported proposal in our public consultations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Members of the public were concerned about the potential abuses of power, as well as the risks faced by volunteers themselves if they were to attempt to confront offenders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Hence, the WALRC will instead rely on a softer approach.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We will galvanise volunteers to educate the public on responsible wildlife practices and discourage the feeding and release of wildlife.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: If volunteers come across offences being committed, they can inform NParks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I will now address the other points raised by Mr Christopher de Souza, Mr Murali Pillai, Ms Anthea Ong, Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Mr Yee Chia Hsing, Miss Cheng Li Hui and Assoc Prof Walter Theseira.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked if the Act would prevent the extermination of pests.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: On the other hand, Miss Cheng Li Hui suggested to remove the burden of proof of intent when it comes to killing, trapping, taking or keeping of wildlife.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: She raised the example of someone who intended to trap a rat but inadvertently caught a Southeast Asian shrew.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I believe the Member thinks that rather than having to consider the intent of a person, we should just prohibit all killing, keeping or taking of wildlife without a permit and leave it only to the professionals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But the implementation of the law has to be practical, balancing wildlife protection with other needs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It would not be reasonable for people to have to call in professionals to handle minor pest issues in their own homes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Further, as shared earlier, there will be safeguards to protect threatened species and our eco-systems.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I agree with Miss Cheng that we should work towards having clear boundaries on what should and should not be done.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The strong public response on this issue has shown me that legislative changes must be complemented with efforts to educate and engage the public.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The law must also be applied sensibly, with the overall objective of creating a set of norms and behaviours around how we interact with wildlife, to more sustainably protect wildlife and ourselves.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This brings me to Mr Murali Pillai's question on whether there should be blanket approval for those who seek to help wildlife out of kindness.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But let me start with some "norm-changing" now.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: If you see an injured wild animal, especially something like an eagle, please call NParks or ACRES instead of attempting to rescue the eagle yourself.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: While we know that many have the best of intentions, untrained human intervention could cause significantly more harm than good.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I understand that NParks is actively building up the capacity and capabilities of the wildlife management industry, so rest assured that there will be trained people ready to provide these necessary services.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Ms Anthea Ong asked if the definition of "wildlife" extends to all wild marine animals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: She also asked if the Act covers the trade of marine wildlife.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: But as Senior Parliamentary Secretary Sun Xueling has explained, NParks also has other existing Acts regulating different aspects of wildlife trade.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: For the amended Wildlife Act, it will be used for regulating wildlife that may cause harm to the public and our local eco-systems.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: For instance, NParks may not want to allow the import of a poisonous jellyfish, without imposing strict conditions to ensure it is not inadvertently released into the wild.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked whether there was an overlap between the prohibition against feeding in the Wildlife Act and the Animals and Birds (Pigeons) Rules.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This will provide more clarity to the public and help us when we engage our residents to tackle the problem of feeding in our neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira asked how the Bill will address wildlife release in religious practices.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I will take it that he is referring to the practice of mercy release in particular.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The WALRC is aware of this practice and that is why we consulted extensively with religious groups.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Mercy release has fallen out of favour with many of them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Captive-bred wildlife, such as those bred for consumption, die quickly in the wild, and those that survive negatively affect our environment and eco-system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: As I have shared in my opening speech, to complement the legislative amendments, the WALRC will continue to work with the community on education and outreach efforts surrounding wildlife release.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Assoc Prof Theseira also asked whether the proposed penalties for the feeding and release of wildlife are appropriate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We took reference from similar offences in other legislation to decide what the appropriate penalty levels would be.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Under the Environmental Public Health Act, repeat littering offenders can be fined up to $10,000.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: These maximum penalties for Court convictions are different from the smaller composition fines that agencies have the discretion to decide on.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Sun Xueling has elaborated on NParks' proposed enforcement approach for feeding and release.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: If the matter goes to the Courts, the Court will consider all the relevant facts and circumstances in deciding the appropriate penalty.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Assoc Prof Theseira also asked under what circumstances would the Director-General (DG) need to grant written approval for feeding wildlife.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: When we rescue injured wild animals, there may be a need to feed them to lure them into traps.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Similarly, during the rehabilitation and release of these rescued wild animals, there might be a need to feed them temporarily after they are released back into the wild.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: These will be carried out by trained professionals and, under the proposed amendments, would require approvals from the Director-General.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: He is right that once we stop the feeding of wild birds, there will likely be a reduction in the number of birds.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The root of the problem here is the availability of food.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: NParks has said, "We have instead focused on methods like managing food waste better and habitat modification, such as the planting of trees that mynahs are less attracted to.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: When food sources are reduced, birds spend more time looking for food and less time mating.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui highlighted that there may be a "loophole" in that someone could claim to be feeding a domestic animal to avoid being prosecuted under section 5A.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I understand this, but I think we must recognise that most feeders, again, are not malicious.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: For many cases, instead of finding ways to punish them under the law, we should be creating more awareness about why they should not be feeding wildlife in the first place.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Both measures have to work hand-in-hand and, together with the other measures NParks is taking, I am confident that we will address the root of the problem and resolve this longstanding issue.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Again, I am extremely happy that the person sitting on the seat I used to sit on is now asking and now repeatedly asking animal-related questions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I do agree with Mr Yee that we need higher penalties to serve as a stronger deterrent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Taken together, these proposed amendments will strengthen our fight against the illegal wildlife trade in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Ms Anthea Ong asked if ordinary citizens could be authorised and given the power to remove and dismantle traps under the new section 10A.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Under the existing section 4(2), the Director-General, subject to the directions of the Board, may only appoint the following persons as "authorised officers": (a) an NParks officer, (b) an employee of another statutory authority, (c) a public officer, or (d) an auxiliary police officer appointed under the Police Force Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: As I have mentioned earlier, the WALRC had considered empowering citizens with certain enforcement powers under the Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: However, we had to balance this against the potential risks, such as to their safety, as enforcement is a challenging business.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: These provisions are not overly prescriptive and only set out the general parameters within which seizure should be effected.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: With regard to forfeiture, while the Courts ultimately make the decision to forfeit a vehicle, NParks must first decide to seize the vehicle.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: If the vehicle is not seized, the forfeiture provision does not apply.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Even if NParks seizes a vehicle to facilitate investigations, I understand that it can still consider whether or not to recommend its forfeiture to the Court.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I trust that NParks will be reasonable in its enforcement and will consider all the relevant facts and circumstances of the case.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: For example, in the case of someone who drives somewhere to feed or release wildlife, the use of the vehicle may be ancillary and not entirely necessary for the commission of an offence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Feeding and release are generally less severe offences in the Wildlife Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: So, seizing a vehicle may not be warranted except in exceptional circumstances.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Compare this to smuggling, which Assoc Prof Walter Theseira raised, where the goods or animals have to be hidden within the conveyances and transported, and where offenders may be dealing with high-value wildlife.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In such cases, the conveyance may need to be seized for a thorough investigation and recommending forfeiture as a punishment would be more proportionate to the crime.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In the case of a private boat operator transporting wildlife for release into the sea, a possible pertinent factor to consider when considering whether forfeiture is warranted would be whether the operator was knowingly abetting illegal activities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: That said, I reiterate that this would depend on the details of the case.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: To clarify, there are also more safeguards other than those under section 12C(2).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Conveyances also cannot be forfeited if they were not proved to have been used in the commission of an offence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Section 12C(4) also adds that conveyances may not be forfeited if the conveyance was unlawfully in the possession of another person without the consent of the owner.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Ultimately, the Court's exercise of discretion will still act as a safeguard.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Thus, I do not feel that additional statutory limits are required at this point.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Sun Xueling has spoken about sentencing policies and NParks' engagement approach.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: These residents may have complex needs, like social isolation or unaddressed mental health issues.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We should be all hands on deck to help them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Of course, there are people who are not supportive and their voices should be heard as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I respect their differing viewpoints and I thank them for taking their time to share their concerns with everyone.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: To start, the proposed controls on feeding attracted the most attention.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Even just a few days ago, people were asking on my Facebook post whether the proposed amendments applied to cats and dogs and asked if it would become illegal to feed community cats and dogs if this Bill is passed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Domestic species of cats and dogs are not covered under this Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: However, it is important to feed responsibly, as leftover food could attract pests and other wildlife.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Others felt that feeding wildlife will cultivate a love for nature and we should not ban it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: For example, one Forum letter read that "People, especially children, develop an interest in the environment through opportunities to interact with animals and birds.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: One of the best ways of doing this is by feeding them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Singaporeans should not be forced to appreciate animals only at a distance." I have provided several reasons for prohibiting the feeding of wildlife in my opening speech.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This is why, for example, we see so many more birds in areas where there is rampant feeding.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It shared that, "Cute squirrels are more common now because more and more people provide them with food".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The result of such feeding is increased human-wildlife conflict.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I cannot put it better than this reply in another Forum letter, "The feeding of nuisance species such as monkeys" – which the original letter writer agreed with – "should be banned, ironically became a nuisance only because people started feeding them." Further, wildlife feeding creates broader problems with the eco-system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Others have also suggested that wildlife feeding could be banned in or near HDB flats, but not in private residential properties.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: To quote, "Why should people living in landed properties face restrictions if they want to attract other desirable wildlife species to their homes?" But the impact of wildlife feeding is not so isolated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: When residents in private properties feed animals, it affects not only themselves but also their neighbours, the animals and the broader eco-system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: There is a solution for those in private residential estates who want to see more wildlife.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: As another letter writer wrote, "We can 'feed' butterflies and birds by planting flowering trees." I agree with that.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: She further states: "In all my decades of observing nature in my backyard or a nearby park, I have never had to provide a single morsel of food to 'attract' wildlife.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: A plethora of garden birds from tiny sunbirds to larger orioles can always be seen throughout the year feeding on naturally-occurring food like nectar, seeds and insects." Someone also emailed me to ask why there is a disparity between the penalties in the Bill and the penalties currently imposed for the feeding of wildlife in our parks and nature reserves.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: He felt that there was no difference whether the person is feeding inside or outside our parks and nature reserves, as both are equally damaging to our natural biodiversity and eco-system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: For parks and gardens, the lower penalties in the Parks and Trees Regulations apply.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Next, I am aware that some feel that since I am mooting this Bill, NGOs will get "special treatment" to do things like provide wildlife removal services.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Like anyone else, NGOs will have to get approval from the DG to release or trap wildlife.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: These provisions are important as they will allow the DG to approve those involved in wildlife rescue efforts, for example, to trap, rescue and subsequently release wildlife in proper places.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: These groups could include NGOs such as ACRES, wildlife management companies and also pest control companies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I can understand these concerns, but any appreciation for nature and wildlife amongst our people must be built on a foundation of safety and respect.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: That comes with keeping a distance and maintaining certain basic boundaries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: As NParks has shared in a Forum letter, there is a huge amount of effort to encourage this responsible interaction.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: They said, "NParks also organises activities and programmes that allow the public to interact responsibly with nature and help foster a love for our environment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Some examples include guided walks, bird-watching and citizen science programmes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: To grow our city in a garden, we will continue to encourage more Singaporeans to be stewards and custodians of our natural heritage, and to coexist harmoniously with wildlife.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We advise the public not to approach, disturb, feed or try to catch wildlife.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It is best to leave them to forage in their natural eco-systems." Sir, allow me to conclude.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The last chapter of this story in amending the Wild Animals and Birds Act is about one important individual – One Giant.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: On 22 October last year, I was about to board my flight back to Singapore when I received the devastating news that Subaraj had passed away that morning.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: He is a friend, a fatherly figure whom I looked up to and a fellow activist.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I just told him recently that my little ones were looking forward to seeing him at Christmas.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: With his long white beard and big belly, Ella thinks he is a Santa Claus.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: He might not be the real Santa Claus but as the media puts it, "he looks a little like Santa Claus, one bearing gifts of knowledge of the wild".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In the words of Minister Desmond Lee, "Subaraj was a true giant and pioneer in our local conservation scene.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: He was larger than life with his long beard and hair and his trademark bandana.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Although he towered over many in his achievements, his demeanour was gentle and his smile always welcoming and reassuring.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Before googling became an easy source of finding information, Subaraj was the Guru who could identify birds by their calls and knew where they could be found.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: If you happened to bump into Subaraj in the forest, where he was often found, he would point out a bird that was hidden from view from everyone else, except him.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: That was his magic, his intimate understanding and his beautiful connection with nature.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: With his passing, we will greatly miss that magic." Subaraj contributed immensely to nature conservation in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: He was undoubtedly one of the most vocal activists, fighting passionately to protect our forests and wildlife.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I met Subaraj's wife, Shamla, who is sitting in the gallery today.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I have no doubt that Subaraj would have been here today to see all of us debating about something so close to his heart, something he has been fighting for and something he devoted his life towards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: At the wake, Shamla told me that whatever Subaraj was helping me with, she will now take over to ensure that his work continues, to ensure that his magic continues.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This is how amazing and selfless Subaraj and his family are.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Even as they grief the loss of a loved one, they never stop thinking about helping others, about their efforts and mission to save the remaining forest and wildlife.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Subaraj had actually suffered a heart attack about a year ago but that never stopped him.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This Wild Animals and Birds (Amendment) Bill is dedicated to you.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It has been a beautiful journey made possible by passionate, selfless individuals who make this world a better place for all.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It has been a privilege chairing this committee and having meetings where we argue passionately, agree to disagree and work together so that we can have a stronger piece of legislation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Later this month, we will publish a post-consultation summary online and on REACH.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, I am happy to introduce this Bill on behalf of the people and animals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have waited a long time to say this.
